text:
"Gerald. "

She was already moving toward the maintenance corridor before the word finished. Marcus followed, not because she asked but because the alternative was standing in the dark alone, and Marcus Reid had already demonstrated that he did not do alone well. The corridor was lit by a single emergency bulb that buzzed like an insect, and Gerald was already at Bessie's panel, his hands moving with the practiced speed of someone who had done this before and hoped he would not have to do it again.

"Grid's down. Not flickering—down. Bessie's starting, but she's going to need a minute. "

"How long? "

"She'sold. She needs to warm up. Like a singer who hasn't performed in a month. "

"I know that feeling. "

Elena ignored him. She pulled out her phone and opened the note she had made earlier—the one with Bessie's capacity, the kitchen-or-broadcast-or-lights decision matrix. The phone's screen was bright in the dark corridor, and she could see Gerald's face in its glow, tired and certain.

"Kitchen first. Refrigeration is already counting down. Broadcast equipment second. Lights last—emergency only. "

"That's what I would've done. "

"I know. But now it's documented. "

She said it without thinking, and the word "documented" hung in the air like a diagnosis. Marcus was leaning against the doorframe, watching her, and she could feel his attention the way she felt changes in barometric pressure—not visible, but undeniable.

"You document everything. "

"Everything that matters. "

"And what doesn't matter? "

"What doesn't matter doesn'tget documented. It gets forgotten. "

Bessie coughed, sputtered, and caught. The generator'shum filled the corridor like a second heartbeat—uneven, labored, but steady. The kitchen lights came on first, then the refrigeration units, then the emergency broadcast equipment in the lobby. Gerald exhaled.

"She's running. Don'task her to do more than she can. "

"I won't. "

They returned to the lobby. The emergency lights made everything look like a photograph—frozen, amber, slightly unreal. Marcus sat at the piano again but did not play. He sat with his hands on the keys, not pressing, just resting, and Elena understood that he was listening to Bessie the way he listened to everything—waiting for the structure to reveal itself.

"I need to make some calls. "

"I know. "

"And I need to—"

"I know. "

She went to her room. The door closed behind her, and the silence was immediate and total, broken only by Bessie's distant hum and the rain's steady percussion against the window. She sat on the bed with her laptop and opened Priya's thread. The messages were stacking up—three since their call, each more urgent than the last. Priya Desai had spent three months aligning investors, and now those investors were asking questions she could not answer.

Elena typed: "Grid is down. Generator running. I'll have a revised timeline by tonight. The pitch is still viable. I'm still viable. " She sent it before she could delete anything, then sat with the word "viable" glowing on the screen. Viable was a word for buildings. She was not a building. But the word felt safer than "okay" or "fine" or "I don't know what I'm doing. "

She opened a new document. At the top she typed: SCOPE OF WORK — WEEKEND. Below it, she began to build the structure she needed—the one that would keep Marcus Reid at a professional distance while they worked through Sunday. The document was absurd. She knew it was absurd. She built it anyway, because absurdity was better than the alternative, which was admitting that she did not know how to be in a room with a man who made her want to stop planning.

The document grew. Section one: logistics. Section two: roles and responsibilities. Section three: communication protocols. Section four: deliverables. Section five: boundaries. She typed "boundaries" and her fingers paused. The word sat on the screen like a door she was not sure she wanted to open.

Section five was where the document broke. She wrote: "Professional distance maintained at all times. No personal disclosure beyond project scope. No physical contact beyond professional necessity. " She stared at the words. They were correct. They were also a lie, because the almost-kiss was not a professional necessity, and the almost-kiss was the thing she could not stop thinking about.

She added a line: "Unscheduled activities: ________________. " The blank was deliberate. She left it empty because filling it would require her to name the thing she wanted, and naming it would make it real, and real things could be stolen. But the empty line glowed on the screen like a question she was not ready to answer.

She saved the document. She did not send it. She sat with it for a long time, listening to Bessie hum and the rain fall and the particular silence of a woman who had just tried to make intimacy auditable and had discovered that the audit itself was the vulnerability.

When she emerged, Marcus was in the lobby with Gerald, looking at the generator panel with the expression of a man who wanted to understand how something worked so he could help but knew his help would be in the way. Gerald was explaining Bessie's quirks—the way she ran hot when the load was uneven, the way she needed to be checked every two hours, the way she sometimes stopped for no reason and needed to be coaxed back.

"She's like a person. She'sgot moods. "

"I know the type. "

Elena approached. Marcus looked up, and she saw him register something—the document on her laptop, the set of her shoulders, the particular tightness around her mouth that meant she had been fighting something and had not won.

"I've drafted a scope of work for the weekend. It covers logistics, roles, deliverables, and boundaries. "

"Boundaries. "

"Professional boundaries. So we both know where the lines are. "

"And where are they? "

Elena opened the laptop and turned it toward him. She watched his eyes move down the document—logistics, roles, communication protocols, deliverables. She watched him reach section five. She watched him read "Professional distance maintained at all times" and "No physical contact beyond professional necessity. " She watched him reach the blank line.

"Unscheduled activities. "

"It's a placeholder. For things we haven't anticipated. "

"Like what? "

"Like anything. Weather changes. Equipment failures. Schedule adjustments. "

"You left it blank. "

"It's a placeholder. It gets filled in as needed. "

"Or it stays blank because you can't name what goes there. "

Elena closed the laptop. The motion was sharp, defensive, and she knew it was defensive, and the knowing made it worse. Marcus did not push. He did not smile. He did not do any of the things she had braced for. He simply stood there, holding her laptop's absence between them like a note he was not going to play.

"I'm not going to sign your scope of work, Elena. "

"It's not a contract. It's a framework. "

"It's a wall. You built it the same way you build everything—neat, numbered, and designed to keep people out. "

"I built it to keep things clear. "

"You built it to keep yourself clear. There's a difference. "

The words landed where she had not fortified, because she had not expected him to refuse. She had expected argument, negotiation, the back-and-forth that she could manage and control. She had not expected him to simply decline, to step outside the framework entirely and leave her standing inside it alone.

"If we don't have boundaries, we don't have—"

"We don't have what? Structure? A plan? A letter? "

"We don't have anything I can rely on. "

"You can rely on me. "

The sentence was simple. It was also the thing she had been running from since Thursday—the thing her father had said before he left, the thing her ex had said before he took her work and called it his own, the thing that every person who had ever left her had said on their way out. "You can rely on me" was not a promise. It was a warning dressed as a comfort.

"I've heard that before. "

"I know. "

"From people who meant it when they said it and didn't mean it when they left. "

"I know that too. "

"Then you understand why I need the document. "

"I understand why you think you need it. I don't think you do. "

Elena looked at him. The lobby was amber and quiet, Bessie humming below, the rain falling outside, and Marcus Reid was standing three feet away with his hands at his sides and his face open in a way that made her want to close something—her laptop, her eyes, the distance between them. She could not do any of these things. She was Elena Marchetti, and she did not close things. She documented them.

"Monday changes things. For both of us. Your tour signature, my pitch. If we—"

"If we what? "

"If we make this something it isn't, and then Monday comes and we're in different cities with different lives, I can't—"

"You can't what? "

"I can't afford to have trusted you. Not with this. Not with me. "

The admission was not what she had planned. It was not in the scope of work, not in the run-of-show, not in any letter she had assigned. It was the thing the blank line had been waiting for, and it had come out not as a word but as a confession, and now it was in the room between them and could not be filed away.

"Elena. "

"Don't. "

"I'm not going to—"

"Don'tsay you understand. Don'tsay you're not going to leave. Don'tsay any of the things that people say when they're about to—"

"I'm not going to leave. "

"You don't know that. "

"Neither do you. That's the point. "

Elena turned and walked toward the elevator. Her legs were steady, her posture correct, her breathing controlled. Everything about her said "professional," and everything about her felt like a woman retreating into a room she had locked from the inside. The elevator doors closed, and she pressed the button for her floor, and the numbers climbed, and she was alone with the hum of Bessie and the rain and the blank line on a document she could not send.

In her room, she sat on the bed with the laptop open. The scope of work stared back at her—every section complete except the one that mattered. She deleted "Professional distance maintained at all times. " She deleted "No physical contact beyond professional necessity. " She left the blank line. She saved the document. She did not send it.

Outside, the storm kept its own time, and Elena Marchetti, who had planned for every letter except this one, lay down in her clothes and stared at the ceiling, and the almost-kiss hung in the dark like a note held past its beat—unfinished, unauthorized, impossible to ignore. The weekend stretched ahead like a piece of music she had not written, and Marcus Reid had already begun to rearrange her measures without asking, and this time she was not sure she wanted him to stop.
